papers.title: Realized Tail-Risk Conditional Autoregressive Expectile Models: Accurate and Stable Forecasting Performance
papers.summary: A realized tail-risk conditional autoregressive expectile (RTCARE) model is proposed for joint forecasting of value-at-risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES). Realized tail measures such as the realized quantile and the realized ES, constructed from intraday high-frequency returns, are incorporated into the dynamics and measurement equations of the conditional expectile, allowing information about lower-tail risk to enter the forecasts. The parameters are estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo, and we evaluate the resulting VaR-ES forecasts in numerical examples and in an empirical application using U.S. stock-return data. Across the considered tail levels, the RTCARE models deliver competitive and often superior forecasting performance relative to existing alternatives, with stable results across Monte Carlo replications and rolling forecast evaluations.

papers.title: Beyond Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Accelerators: Directed Evidence for Adaptive Sustainability Portfolios
papers.summary: Governments and development partners often seek Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) "accelerators" whose progress can propagate gains across human well-being, institutions, resources, and environmental priorities. Such claims require evidence on direction, timing, robustness, and trade-offs, not only network connectivity. We map directed SDG interdependence using a balanced panel of 114 countries observed annually from 2000 to 2024. Because the goal series are persistent, trending, and cross-sectionally dependent, we combine Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger non-causality tests on first-differenced series with false-discovery control across 272 directed goal pairs, and panel local projections with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors for 31 theory-derived indicator linkages. We find 84 directed linkages after correction: 40 synergies and 44 trade-offs. This dense structure does not support a universal accelerator. Driver-receiver rankings are fragile across lag orders, centrality metrics, bootstrap resampling, and alternative dependence controls; only peace and strong institutions as a net receiver and poverty reduction as an effect-size-weighted driver are distinguishable in the bootstrap screen. Two local-projection pathways are supported, both leading to lower child mortality, and the education-child-health association is corroborated in independent World Development Indicators data across 183 countries. The policy implication is not to abandon SDG integration, but to replace fixed global accelerator rankings with adaptive portfolios built around supported, time-lagged linkages and monitored constituent indicators.

papers.title: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction
papers.summary: Score-based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian noise, corresponding to a light-tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction: limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy-tailed, bursty, and occasionally jump-like. We study STOCHLOB, a training-only score-matching framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the deployed predictor deterministic. Instead of Brownian-only Gaussian corruption, the noising process uses two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired alternatives: jump-Lévy noise through a compound-Poisson variance mixture, and clipped $α$-stable noise through a positive-stable Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and heavy-tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse-time diffusion sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful interpretation: its radial factor $h_t(r)$ is the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. On chronologically held-out Coinbase LOB data, the proposed variants remain competitive on uncorrupted BTC and altcoin test horizons and improve several realized tail-window stress diagnostics. An exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction costs and trading-rule constraints. Code and configuration files are available at https://github.com/ArshiAbolghasemi/Penny.

papers.title: Testing for an Explosive Bubble using High-Frequency Volatility
papers.summary: Based on a continuous-time stochastic volatility model with a linear drift, we develop a test for explosive behavior in financial asset prices at a low frequency when prices are sampled at a higher frequency. The test exploits the volatility information in the high-frequency data. The method consists of devolatizing log-asset price increments with realized volatility measures and performing a supremum-type recursive Dickey-Fuller test on the devolatized sample. The proposed test has a nuisance-parameter-free asymptotic distribution and is easy to implement. We study the size and power properties of the test in Monte Carlo simulations. A real-time date-stamping strategy based on the devolatized sample is proposed for the origination and conclusion dates of the explosive regime. Conditions under which the real-time date-stamping strategy is consistent are established. The test and the date-stamping strategy are applied to study explosive behavior in cryptocurrency and stock markets.

papers.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO
papers.summary: LASSO is one of the most popular regularization methods for high-dimensional regression models. While cointegration is common in practical applications of predictive regressions with many regressors, the convex penalty of LASSO overly suppresses the coefficients of cointegrated regressors and therefore fails to deliver consistent parameter estimation. We employ folded concave penalties (FCP), including the well-known SCAD and MCP, to address this issue. Using FCP, we establish two asymptotic results: (i) a local oracle property for the penalized regression, and (ii) a global oracle property for regressions with a penalty-level constraint. In particular, the latter guarantees a global solution that consistently estimates the true coefficients and enjoys oracle prediction performance. Simulation studies and an application to predicting the euro area unemployment rate show that FCP improves variable selection and out-of-sample prediction relative to LASSO.

papers.title: ACT, WAIT, or EXPERIMENT: A Causal Governance Framework for Retail Price Optimization Under Abstentions
papers.summary: This paper presents a causal decision framework for list-price elasticities in intermediated retail channels, where estimates are confounded by promotions, competitor moves and shopkeeper pass-through. Rather than forcing a number when the evidence is ambiguous, the system treats abstention (Wait) as an active diagnostic output. Built on Double Machine Learning and conformal prediction, it evaluates whether conditions exist to act on a recommended price or whether withholding is preferable, and it states when: acting beats withholding exactly when the calibration slope of the true headroom on the recommended move exceeds one half, a condition that predicts the sign of the gain in 37 of 38 synthetic groups. When the system abstains, it classifies the cause and flags which products are candidates for a designed pricing experiment. Aggregating estimates to the brand or category level, where independent price designs average out, cuts the root mean squared error from 0.488 to 0.159, although aggregation alone does not make the intervals honest. Tested on synthetic data with known truth and on public scanner data, the study reports its costs: the system abstains on 52% to 87% of presentations that were identifiable, and a single-window estimate forecasts real price changes poorly (calibration slope 0.22). What it offers is a way to audit any abstention rule and to publish at the unit the evidence supports; no commercial panel or pilot was used, so it does not measure commercial uplift.

papers.title: An Averaging Alternative to Pre-Trend Testing
papers.summary: We study difference-in-differences (DID) estimation of average treatment effects on the treated when the researcher is uncertain about which pre-treatment periods satisfy the parallel trends assumption. Roth (2022) shows that pre-trend testing can induce bias, complementing the statistical literature on post-selection inference. We propose the model averaged difference-in-differences (MADID) estimator, a weighted average of the candidate $2\times2$ DID estimators. The weights are normalized exponential functions of the candidate residual sums of squares, so implementation requires no specification test. We derive MADID's asymptotic properties under conditions that make invalid comparisons detectably more variable than at least one valid comparison. Under these conditions, MADID is consistent when the parallel trends assumption holds for at least one pre-treatment period. Although its joint limiting distribution across post-treatment periods is generally non-Gaussian, inference can be conducted by subsampling or simulation.

papers.title: Intentionally Overidentifying Local Projections
papers.summary: Local projections (LPs) have become a standard tool for estimating dynamic effects in macroeconomics and are typically implemented using ordinary least squares (OLS) for a given lag order. We propose an alternative approach that exploits additional lags as excluded instrumental variables (IVs). Under a finite-order model with martingale-difference shocks, the resulting (optimally weighted) IV estimator is never asymptotically less efficient than OLS and, as we show, can deliver substantial efficiency gains when data are persistent. For the unit-root AR(1) data with i.i.d. errors, our baseline IV estimator (with one overidentifying restriction) has asymptotic variance $2-h^{-1}$, compared with $h$, the asymptotic variance of the OLS lag-augmented estimator in Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2021), for an integer propagation horizon $h$. We then develop IV-based LP inference that is robust to unknown persistence and moderate local model misspecification, whereas the recursive VAR-based inference is generally not robust to the latter. We also characterize the trade-off between the degree of misspecification and the number of additional lag controls. Through simulations and an empirical application, we demonstrate that the proposed method can yield meaningfully shorter confidence intervals for impulse responses than OLS in finite samples.

papers.title: Volatility in Prediction Markets: A Structural Approach
papers.summary: Forward-looking volatility forecasts are central inputs to derivatives pricing, market making, risk management, and volatility-linked trading strategies, with ARCH and GARCH models serving as the canonical workhorses. Such models are natural in standard asset markets, where prices are positive-valued stochastic processes and volatility is typically inferred from return dynamics. Prediction markets have a different structure: prices are bounded probabilities, payoffs are binary, and contracts resolve at known deadlines. We develop and estimate a volatility model tailored to binary prediction markets. The model combines two economic mechanisms: a Wright-Fisher deadline-resolution component, capturing how remaining binary uncertainty is forced to resolve over time, and a Glosten-Milgrom order-flow component, capturing volatility from informed trading as reflected in spreads and volume. Using a large panel of Kalshi contracts, we show that these structural variables carry substantial forecasting power. Plain ARCH/GARCH benchmarks are dominated by structural specifications; scaling the structural variance by a GARCH multiplier gives the best overall forecasts.The two layers play distinct roles: the structural term sets the level of conditional variance, while the GARCH recursion corrects the timing of interval violations.The model also provides an interpretable measurement framework: volatility is highest near fifty-fifty prices, rises near resolution, and varies across categories with the timing and discreteness of information arrival. Economics contracts are closer to smooth deadline-resolution dynamics, while sports contracts exhibit more event-concentrated, jump-like behavior. Across major categories, re-estimating the model within each category does not improve out-of-sample performance, suggesting that the pooled structural specification transfers beyond the headline result.

papers.title: Discrete-Time Survival Modelling with Dynamic Industrial Graphs for Mortgage Credit Risk
papers.summary: Mortgage credit risk may exhibit dependence across economically connected areas, even when they are geographically distant. However, current models typically represent cross-area dependence through fixed geographical neighbourhoods, potentially overlooking economic connections that extend beyond physical proximity and evolve over time. These models may fail to capture shared risks among geographically distant but economically similar areas, and cannot describe a changing dependence of risk; it therefore risks retaining economically obsolete connections while omitting newly emerging ones. This paper uses similarities of industrial composition as a measure of economic proximity and develops a discrete-time survival model with dynamic industrial graphs to capture evolving cross-area dependence in mortgage default risk. The resulting graphs are reconstructed annually, allowing both their topology and edge weights to change as regional industrial compositions evolve. Jointly combining a proper conditional autoregressive process with a first-order autoregressive process governs the temporal cross-area dependence and the temporal persistence in latent risk simultaneously. The model is estimated using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation and evaluated on U.S. mortgage loan-level data against the static industrial graph specifications. The results show that the proposed dynamic model achieves better in-sample fit and out-of-sample discrimination, while its estimated parameters indicate substantial graph-induced cross-area dependence and temporal persistence. These findings demonstrate the value of allowing economically defined neighbourhoods to evolve when modelling mortgage default risk.

papers.title: Synthetic Control under Out-of-Span Common Shocks: Diagnosis, Exposure Balance and Correction
papers.summary: Synthetic control relies on pre-treatment fit to balance the unobserved factors that drive untreated outcomes. Balancing an observed exposure index removes the problem, but simplex weights can achieve balance only when the treated unit lies inside the donors' exposure hull. Outside the hull, every simplex-weighted estimator carries an exposure imbalance with an explicit lower bound. Iran's 2012 sanctions coincided with the 2014 oil collapse, and Iran is more oil-dependent than any of its natural comparators. The 2012-15 output loss of about 12 percent survives every adjustment. papers.title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO
papers.summary: Estimating the first stage of an instrumental variables (IV) model with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) requires choosing a dictionary of technical instruments and a penalty level. papers.title: Neural Estimation of Irreversibility in Real and Simulated Limit Order Book Paths
papers.summary: A path indistinguishable from its own reverse carries no arrow of time, so time irreversibility is a necessary condition for a directed mechanism to be readable from trajectories alone. A surrogate preserving the coarse one-step transition table recovers 30 percent less irreversibility than the observed paths. The increment is positive for all twelve symbols on every held-out daytime date, and for NVDA in each session window. It changes more than tenfold with the coarse-graining scale. Neither a linear score nor any single feature group reproduces the full fitted rate. papers.title: E-Backtesting Expected Shortfall without Value-at-Risk Forecasts under Time-series Models
papers.summary: Expected Shortfall (ES) measures the average size of tail losses. Its sequential backtests typically also require a Value-at-Risk (VaR) forecast. papers.summary: Causal discovery in time series is increasingly performed using nonlinear machine-learning models, yet the resulting causal relationships are almost always summarized by scalar edge scores. papers.title: Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models
papers.summary: When a trader executes a large order, the relevant question is not \emph{what will the price be?} but \emph{what would the price have been had I not traded?} Market impact is thus a causal quantity, yet classical models (Almgren--Chriss, propagators) regress price on flow, which is biased whenever informed flow moves prices through information as well as trading. papers.title: Bayesian heterogeneous copula mixtures with nonparametric margins: consistency, identifiability and tail asymmetry in physical fitness data
papers.summary: Finite mixtures of Clayton, Gumbel, Frank and Gaussian copulas can describe dependence that differs between the upper and lower tails. papers.title: On integrability of local utility maximizing strategies
papers.summary: In stochastic control problems involving optimal portfolio choice, one often seeks an optimizer of some local criterion (dynamic programming value function) generated by some global criterion (e.g., expected utility). It is shown that the reasonable asymptotic elasticity condition of Kramkov and Schachermayer (1999) applied to the local utility function plays a key role in this context.

papers.title: Designing Independent Variation: A Guided Iteration Methodology for Price Experiments in Short, Correlated Panels
papers.summary: Estimation error in short, correlated pricing panels is dominated by trajectory dispersion rather than sampling noise, creating an identification shortfall that only independently assigned variation can resolve. We propose a guided iteration methodology to decide how much variation to generate, where, and for how long: a cyclic price-perturbation scheme under a revenue-at-risk budget, framed as variance minimization over design-specific error covariances, analogous to portfolio selection. We establish four key results: (1) a closed-form minimum-variance combination rule; (2) proof that a convex cost of intensity yields an interior, spread-out allocation, whereas under a concave tolerable-volume-loss cost, concentrating intensity into fewer perturbations pays off only with heterogeneous candidates, priced-in fixed costs, or perturbations beyond the cost curve's inflection point; (3) a discounted recursion yielding a data-dependent exit timeline from the experimentation zone; and (4) an application to Dominick's retail data, in which about five designed independent units match the precision of approximately 700 passive equivalents in the anchor category, while a fast proxy across ten categories achieves a median 97% variance reduction relative to passive panels. Sixteen comparisons (eleven pre-specified) support the theory: greedy selection achieves 90-93% of the global optimum across more than fifty exhaustively verifiable instances, and the recursion reaches its predicted 90%-of-steady-state benchmark two cycles early, though a parametric bootstrap indicates that its delta-method interval understates the right-tail risk. Boundary conditions show that regularized covariance estimators extend plug-in noise tolerance from 29% to beyond 50%, submodularity holds up to a clear curvature threshold, and a shared shock imposes a fundamental precision floor.

papers.title: Measuring intraday return-shape geometry with modified Brownian motion
papers.summary: Realised kurtosis measures intraday tail risk but compresses the shape of the return distribution into a single scalar, so trading days with similar kurtosis may differ in how probability mass is spread across the peak, the shoulders and the tails. We propose a geometric description of intraday return shape based on the modified Brownian motion model (MBMM), which deforms a Gaussian benchmark through a nonlinear feedback governed by a shape parameter and a distortion intensity. Our main contribution is a peak-shoulder-tail decomposition that measures where the fitted return density gains or loses probability mass relative to the Gaussian, complemented by two feedback landmarks that explain how the shape parameter generates these deformations. We estimate the model at the stock-day level using a bin-free simulation-based minimum-distance estimator that matches empirical and model-implied intraday quantiles, and we document its finite-sample reliability by Monte Carlo. Using regular session one-minute returns for ten liquid U.S. stocks from May 2021 to April 2026, we find that the MBMM provides a substantially better in-sample fit than geometric Brownian motion on every estimator-ready stock-day, and that days with closely matched realised kurtosis can display materially different peak-shoulder-tail geometries. Finally, we show that the estimated shape parameters behave as persistent daily state variables: they are strongly forecastable relative to a random-walk benchmark, though their predictability reflects persistence around a slowly moving level rather than rich autoregressive dynamics. The proposed decomposition offers a risk-shape measurement layer that complements realised kurtosis by describing not only how large intraday tail risk is, but how it is formed, giving investors and risk managers additional distributional information for risk monitoring and, potentially, prediction.

papers.title: Principal component error in high-dimensional factor models
papers.summary: In a statistical factor model, principal components (or eigenvectors) of a sample covariance matrix serve as estimates of principal directions, the true drivers of co-movement of a collection of observed variables. We write the often substantial error in these estimates as a sum of two interpretable terms, which we show have almost sure asymptotic limits as the number of variables grows with sample size bounded. This scenario is commonplace in financial economics, genomics, machine learning and signal processing. Out-of-subspace error measures the distance from an estimate to the subspace spanned by population factor exposures. It can be expressed in terms of data, providing an estimable floor for asymptotic error. In-subspace error is driven by a rotation error within that subspace, which arises from the fixed sample size of the latent factor returns and cannot be estimated from data alone. We illustrate our error analysis with a three-factor simulation of the US public equity market, showing the dependence of the magnitude of the error and its components on dimension and sample size. In that simulation, out-of-subspace error dominates. Researchers who rely on principal component analysis to estimate factor models can use our results to quantify errors in model-based predictions and attributions.

papers.title: Instrumental Variable Analysis in Underrepresented Subpopulations Powered by Knowledge Transfer
papers.summary: Instrumental variable (IV) analysis in underrepresented target populations suffers from low statistical efficiency and weak IV bias due to limited sample size. Leveraging external knowledge from a source population with larger samples offers an appealing solution to this problem. KNIVES constructs a knowledge-transferred IV score by combining multiple candidate models through an effective signal-to-noise ratio criterion tailored to the downstream IV estimator, rather than prediction accuracy alone. To address weak associations between the IV score and the exposure, as well as a high correlation among candidate models in the target population, KNIVES employs a bias correction technique to mitigate the resulting bias and ensure robust performance. Theoretical investigation demonstrates that our method is robust to weak IV bias and achieves improved efficiency compared to the causal effect estimator based on any single candidate model. In addition, KNIVES avoids negative transfer by guaranteeing that its asymptotic variance is not larger than that of the estimator relying solely on target population data. Extensive numerical studies demonstrate the superior finite-sample performance of our method over existing methods. Two Mendelian randomization studies on ethnic minority subgroups in UK Biobank data further illustrate the advantages of our method.

papers.title: Nonlinear fiscal multiplier controlling for policy and economic regimes
papers.summary: A new form of the fiscal multiplier suited to data expressed as gross growth rates is proposed, together with a structural vector autoregression that isolates discretionary fiscal policy from regime and rule-based components. Because cumulating growth-rate responses over a horizon involves a product rather than a sum, the proposed multiplier is multiplicative: both numerator and denominator are polynomials in the size of the fiscal impulse, so the multiplier varies nonlinearly with the scale of the expenditure programme -- a dependence that conventional additive multipliers cannot capture. The multiplier requires no discounting, no ad hoc conversion factor, and no auxiliary estimate of an average expenditure share of output, and it is computed directly from nominal, non-seasonally-adjusted data, matching the terms in which government budgets are actually expressed. A version of the narrative approach to identification is introduced. It allows to decompose the influence of fiscal policy into a regime component, a standard policy rule embedded in the autoregressive structure, and discretionary shocks. Removing the regime component from the residuals yields smaller identified shocks, and correspondingly smaller multipliers, than found in SVARs not controlling for regime changes -- closing much of the gap between SVAR- and DSGE-based estimates. It is found that multipliers vary substantially across countries and across types of government expenditure, that regime volatility itself differs markedly by country, and that several economies display cyclicality in spending and multiplier paths that only becomes visible once responses are cumulated multiplicatively. The resulting multipliers are nominal, derived from unadjusted data, proven to be sensitive to shock size, and purged of regime effects, offering a tool with direct relevance for budget planning and fiscal policy evaluation.

papers.title: A Structural Matrix Autoregression Framework for International Spillovers
papers.summary: Understanding how macroeconomic shocks propagate across countries requires structural models that can jointly identify country-specific shocks and their international transmission. Yet extending structural vector autoregressions (SVARs) to large multi-country systems is challenging due to rapidly increasing dimensionality, computational costs, and the proliferation of identifying restrictions. This paper develops a Bayesian Structural Matrix Autoregression (BSMAR) framework that exploits the natural matrix structure of international macroeconomic data. By separating dependence across economic variables from dependence across countries, the framework provides a parsimonious representation that substantially reduces the dimensionality of large structural systems. We develop a Bayesian sampling algorithm for posterior inference that accommodates zero, sign, and ranking (magnitude) restrictions, allowing established SVAR identification schemes to be combined with a novel approach to identifying contemporaneous international spillovers. Applying the model to quarterly data for 15 economies, we find substantial heterogeneity in international shock transmission, with demand shocks playing a more prominent role than supply shocks in generating cross-country spillovers.

papers.title: CoCopula: Conformal Calibration and Copula Aggregation for Reliable Renewable Energy Forecasting
papers.summary: The rapid growth of renewable energy penetration has intensified the need for reliable probabilistic forecasts to support grid operations at aggregated (fleet or system) levels. In practice, however, system operators often lack access to fleet-level probabilistic models and instead rely on site-level forecasts produced by heterogeneous third-party providers. Constructing coherent and calibrated fleet-level probabilistic forecasts from such inputs remains challenging due to complex cross-site dependencies and aggregation-induced miscalibration. Motivated by a real-world operational challenge identified through collaboration with an industry partner, this paper presents a probabilistic aggregation and calibration framework that directly converts site-level probabilistic forecasts into reliable fleet-level forecasts. The paper introduces \method~ (\textbf{Co}nformal Calibration and \textbf{Copula} Aggregation), which integrates Copula-based dependence modeling to capture cross-site correlations followed by Context-Aware Conformal Prediction (CACP) to mitigate miscalibration at the aggregated level. This combination enables dependence-aware aggregation while improving empirical coverage and maintaining sharp prediction intervals. Experiments on large-scale solar generation datasets from three system operators in the United States including MISO, ERCOT, and SPP demonstrate that the proposed \method{} approach achieves near-nominal empirical coverage and consistently lower Winkler scores than competing aggregation-based baselines across different target coverage levels. Importantly, \method{} achieves performance comparable to directly calibrated system-level forecasts, demonstrating its practical value when dedicated fleet-level forecasting models are unavailable.
